questions.title: Gravitational potential of a planet — surface g & satellite orbit period

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to that point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: Reading from Fig. 1.1 at x = 4800 km = 4.8 × 10⁶ m: φ = −3.55 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.answer:
From φ = −GM/r, r = −GM/φ = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.55 × 10²⁴ / (0.65 × 10⁷) = 2.6 × 10⁷ m (range 2.60–2.65 × 10⁷ m).
For the fixed (geostationary-type) orbit GMm/r² = mω²r with ω = 2π/T, giving T² = 4π²r³/GM = 4.20 × 10⁹ s².
T = 64 800 s = 18 hours

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
Similarity (any one): inversely proportional to distance (from the point mass/charge); points of equal potential lie on concentric spheres; zero at infinite distance.
Difference (any one): gravitational potential is always negative, whereas electric potential can be positive or negative.

questions.title: Ideal gas — pV = NkT check, first law, molecular kinetic energy & condensation energy

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: An ideal gas is a gas that obeys pV ∝ T, where T is the thermodynamic (absolute) temperature.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: Using pV/T = constant (with T in kelvin): initial pV/T = 1.10 × 10⁵ × 540 × 10⁻⁶ / 300 = 0.198, and final pV/T = 6.70 × 10⁶ × 30 × 10⁻⁶ / 1015 = 0.198. The two values are equal, so the helium behaves as an ideal gas.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: No thermal energy enters or leaves, so q = 0. From ΔU = q + W, ΔU = W. Work is done <u>on</u> the gas (its volume decreases), so the internal energy — and hence the temperature — increases.

questions.title: Oscillating mass on a spring — energy lines, period & damping

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: P: total energy; Q: potential energy; R: kinetic energy.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer:
From Fig. 3.2 the total energy E = 6.4 mJ and the amplitude x₀ = 1.6 cm.
E = ½mω²x₀², so ω² = 2E/(mx₀²) = 2 × 6.4 × 10⁻³ / (0.130 × 0.016²) = 438, giving ω = 20.9 rad s⁻¹.
T = 2π/ω = 2π/20.9 = 0.30 s

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: Resistive forces (such as air resistance) acting on the oscillating object.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer:
After each oscillation the energy is multiplied by 0.92, so after 6 oscillations the energy remaining = 6.4 × 0.92⁶ = 3.9 mJ.
Decrease in total energy = 6.4 − 3.9 = 2.5 mJ

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.answer: Light damping, because the amplitude decreases only gradually (the system continues to oscillate for many cycles).

questions.title: Coulomb's law — equilibrium of a charged sphere, electric potential energy & electron between plates

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The electric force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: On sphere Y: tension acting upwards along the thread, weight acting vertically downwards, and the electric (repulsive) force acting horizontally to the right — all three correctly labelled.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer:
F_E = Q₁Q₂/(4πε₀r²) = (96 × 10⁻⁹ × 64 × 10⁻⁹)/(4π × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 0.080²) = 8.63 × 10⁻³ N.
The thread makes angle θ with the vertical, where sin θ = 0.080/1.2 = 0.0667, so θ = 3.82°.
Resolving: T sin θ = F_E and T cos θ = mg, hence tan θ = F_E/mg.
m = F_E/(g tan θ) = 8.63 × 10⁻³/(9.81 × tan 3.82°) = 0.013 kg

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: Towards plate P (towards the top of the page), since the electron is attracted to the positive plate.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.answer: The force is always in the same direction (towards the positive plate) rather than always perpendicular to the velocity, so the electron follows a parabolic path, not a circular one.

questions.title: Capacitor discharge — capacitance from ln Q graph, resistance & stored energy

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer:
At t = 0 the capacitor is fully charged, so Q₀ = CV = 12C. From the graph ln Q = 2.9, so Q₀ = e²·⁹ = 18.2 μC.
C = Q/V = 18.2/12 = 1.5 μF

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer:
The gradient of the ln Q – t graph is −1/RC = −0.25.
R = 1/(0.25 × 1.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.7 × 10⁶ Ω

parts.label: (d)
parts.answer:
The second resistor in parallel halves the total resistance, so the time constant RC halves and the gradient doubles.
Sketch a straight line starting from (0, 2.9) with twice the (negative) gradient, drawn between t = 0 and at least t = 5.0 s.

questions.title: Hall probe — orientation, silicon vs copper & induced e.m.f. in a coil

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The Hall voltage is zero when the plane of the probe is parallel to the (magnetic) field lines, and maximum when the plane of the probe is perpendicular to the field lines.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: n is the number density of charge carriers (the number of charge carriers per unit volume).

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: Silicon has a much smaller value of n than copper, so for the same B, I, t and q the Hall voltage V_H is much greater, making the probe more sensitive.

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
A Hall reading of 36 mV corresponds to B = (36/24) × 32 = 48 mT.
The flux density changes by ΔB = 48 mT in Δt = 1.4 s (between 7.2 s and 8.6 s).
E = ΔΦ/Δt = ΔB·A·N/Δt = (48 × 10⁻³ × π × 0.018² × 780)/1.4 = 0.027 V

questions.title: Hydrogen energy levels — absorption spectrum & photon energy

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Photons of particular wavelengths are absorbed by electrons in the cool gas, exciting them to higher energy levels. The photon energy must equal the difference between two energy levels, so only certain discrete wavelengths are absorbed. The excited electrons then de-excite, re-emitting photons in all directions, so those wavelengths are largely removed from the forward beam, producing dark (absorption) lines.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer:
For the 658 nm line: photon energy = hc/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ / (658 × 10⁻⁹) = 3.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 1.89 eV.
This photon is emitted in the transition n = 3 → n = 2, so E₃ − E₂ = 1.89 eV. With E₂ = −3.40 eV, E₃ = −1.51 eV = −1.51 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = −2.42 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

questions.title: Plutonium-238 alpha decay — activity, power output & half-life

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: ²³⁸₉₄Pu → ²³⁴₉₂U + ⁴₂α (uranium-234 and an alpha particle).

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer: Power = activity × energy per decay = 5.54 × 10¹⁴ × 5.59 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 496 W

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.answer:
Power ∝ activity ∝ e^(−λt), so 0.653 = e^(−λt).
ln 0.653 = −(ln 2/87.7)t, giving t = 53.9 years

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
Advantage: much less mass is needed (3.37 g instead of 0.874 kg), so less energy is needed to launch the probe.
Disadvantage: the half-life is much shorter, so it would not provide power for as long.

questions.title: Ultrasound — detection, V₀ & ω, acoustic impedance of soft tissue

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Ultrasound is detected by a piezo-electric crystal. The ultrasound wave causes the crystal to vibrate (change shape), and this change of shape generates an e.m.f., which is detected.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: Z = ρc, so its unit is kg m⁻³ × m s⁻¹ = kg m⁻² s⁻¹

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.answer: The acoustic impedances of air (4.3 × 10² kg m⁻² s⁻¹) and soft tissue (1.7 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹) are very different, so the intensity reflection coefficient ≈ 1. Almost no ultrasound is transmitted into the air-filled cavity, so no image can be formed.

questions.title: Stellar brightness, standard candles & Hubble's law

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Some stars appear brighter because they are closer to the Earth, and some appear brighter because they have a greater luminosity (in the visible region).

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: A standard candle is an object (star) of known luminosity.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.answer: The observed wavelength is greater than the laboratory wavelength, so the light is redshifted. The star (and its galaxy) is therefore moving away from the Earth. This is evidence that the Universe is expanding.
